The US Government Is Letting a Key Data Center Regulation Expire

The federal government is planning to let a rule regulating federal data center operations sunset in September with no replacement.

The US government is quietly planning to allow a rule outlining the standards for federal data center usage and operations, known as the Federal Data Center Enhancement Act (FDCEA), to expire, according to sources who spoke to WIRED. Neither Congress nor the Trump administration appears to be making significant moves to protect or extend the rule, or put alternate plans in place.

Data centers have become a hot-button issue in recent months, as the tech industry goes all in on artificial intelligence and the infrastructure needed to power it. According to a Gallup poll from May, more than 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of data centers, the energy- and water-intensive buildings that power the AI boom, in their communities. From Utah to Georgia, residents across the political spectrum have united to voice their resistance to the data center build-out.

Despite the public backlash, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), the government agency that sets guidance for how agencies implement policies in line with the president’s agenda, is not providing any plans for how federal agencies should manage the sunset or continue to implement reporting beyond the timeline of the law. This, current and former workers at OMB and the General Services Administration (GSA) say, signals that the Trump administration is set to take an even more hands-off approach to data center oversight and regulation...

💡 The world’s largest data center just got approved in a Utah county of 60,000 people.

Three commissioners voted yes. The public watched on a livestream.
That’s the reality of how fast AI infrastructure is moving—and it’s sparking a debate every business leader needs to pay attention to.

Here’s what’s happening:
Kevin O’Leary’s “Stratos Project” in Box Elder County, Utah spans 40,000 acres and is on track to become the world’s largest data center. The total investment is projected to exceed $100 billion, with the first gigawatt of capacity expected to be operational within two years.

The business case is straightforward: AI needs compute. Compute needs land, power, and speed.

But here’s where it gets complicated for the rest of us in business:
⚡ The energy demand is staggering.
The Utah project would require more than double the electricity the entire state currently consumes in a year. O’Leary says the facility will generate its own power—but that scale should make every CFO think twice about energy cost projections in their own region.
💧 Water is the new oil.
Residents worry the water needed to cool the facility could further strain the nearby Great Salt Lake, whose level has already fallen 22 feet since 1986. Water scarcity is no longer just an ESG talking point—it’s a site-selection variable.
🏛️ Community relations can make or break a project.
In Festus, Missouri, voters replaced every incumbent up for reelection after their town council approved a $6 billion data center project. Maine lawmakers passed an 18-month ban on data center development, though Governor Janet Mills ultimately vetoed it. The backlash is real and it’s bipartisan, even when it doesn’t stick.
📈 The economic upside is undeniable . . . if managed well.
At full buildout, the Stratos Project could deliver $108 million in annual revenue to Box Elder County from the energy and data center complex alone. That’s a transformative number for a rural community. But full buildout is years away, and trust needs to be built alongside the infrastructure.

The O’Leary-Utah story isn’t just about one data center. It’s a preview of the infrastructure battles that will define the next decade of AI growth—and the communities, investors, and companies that navigate them well will have a serious competitive advantage.

The question isn’t whether data centers will be built. It’s whether they’ll be built with or without the communities they depend on.

What’s your take — is this the cost of AI progress, or is there a smarter way to scale?

Everyone's bullish on AI until the actual data center wants to move in next door. Then we all become NIMBYs.

Here's what I've been thinking about, living in the Salt Lake City Valley below the upcoming Project Stratos.

For people who don't live in northern Utah, Stratos is a controversial hyperscale data center project going up in Box Elder County. 

Reporting puts it at multi-gigawatt scale, one of the largest AI infrastructure builds in the country. 

The water draw is significant. The power demand is significant. 

And it's being built in a state where the Great Salt Lake has lost roughly two-thirds of its surface area in the last 40 years.

This is not a unique story. Versions of Stratos are being approved in Virginia, Arizona, Texas, Wyoming. The map of America is being redrawn for compute demands. Your time will be next.

Now zoom in on the other side of this project.

What is the average professional actually using AI for right now? Meeting notes. Email rewrites. Research summaries. A small percentage of people are doing genuinely novel work. 

Most are not. Most are unaware of the planetary-scale infrastructure they are tapping into to save 20 minutes a day on writing an email to their contacts.

I don't think AI is a fad. I think it will reshape entire industries. I'm not anti-progress. Its definitely here to stay.

But I think the loudest people in this conversation have skipped over a real question.

What is the actual cost beyond your monthly usage subscription?

How many gallons of water and megawatts of power are we willing to spend per unit of human output? At what point does the math stop working? And who gets to decide, when the people most affected by the tradeoff are not the ones writing the LinkedIn posts about how transformative this all is?

Here in Utah the people don't get to opt out. Utah's water table doesn't get to opt out.

Saying yes to the future is fine. Pretending it's free is not. 

Open debate and comments welcome.

Infrastructure firm O'Leary Digital has exclusively revealed the first images of the Stratos Hyperscale Data Center in Box Elder County, Utah, which is being designed by architecture studio Gensler as one of the largest data centers in the world.

The development is set to contain 60 data centers on an initial 10,000-acre portion of the site. The master plan shows six data center clusters spaced out, with a buffer along the property edge, solar arrays, and a mixed-use innovation district.

Rendering of the structure shows buildings with a similar design language to the Wonder Valley data center in Canada, also designed by Gensler. 

#ProjectsWeAdmire

Box Elder County is currently standing on the precipice of a decision that could reshape Northern Utah’s landscape forever. The proposed Stratos Project — a massive, 40,000-acre data center and energy campus — is larger than Bryce Canyon National Park. But its physical footprint pales in comparison to its staggering resource demands.

At full operation, the facility will require 9 gigawatts (GW) of electricity. To put that in perspective, the entire state of Utah operates on a continuous demand of about 4 GW. Stratos alone will demand more than double the entire state’s power grid capacity, a deficit the developers plan to plug by burning natural gas directly on-site.

The scale of this project is unprecedented, yet local democratic oversight is being entirely hollowed out. Rather than proceeding through ordinary county zoning, Stratos is utilizing the Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA). This state-authorized framework strips away local control, superseding standard municipal zoning laws and allowing MIDA to capture local property tax increments.

With traditional zoning off the table, the regulatory battleground has shifted to our most fragile resource: water. Simultaneously, a newly passed state law, HB 60, has narrowed the State Engineer’s water-rights review, limiting broad “public welfare” arguments and weakening generalized community objections.

Utah Clean Energy’s modeling shows that the project presents a devastating environmental trade-off depending on how those generators are built:

* The Water Crisis: If the project uses Combined-Cycle Combustion Turbines (CCCT), it will require 50,000 acre-feet of water annually. At a time when the Great Salt Lake desperately needs an extra 800,000 acre-feet per year just to reach a healthy elevation, diverting this vital resource directly threatens the lake’s recovery and further depletes the vulnerable Hansel Valley aquifer

* The Air Quality Crisis: If the developers choose Reciprocating Internal Combustion Engines (RICE) to save water, they will instead trigger an air quality disaster. This configuration would increase Utah’s climate-warming CO2 emissions by 75% and emit 12,000 tons of nitrogen oxides (NOx) per year. Prevailing winds would carry this massive pollution cloud south, dumping it straight into the Wasatch Front and pushing the region entirely out of compliance with federal Clean Air Act standards.

Closed-loop cooling can cut a data center's water use by 90%. So why is Utah's biggest data center fight still about water?

Every data center developer I talk to leads with the cooling number.

And the number is genuinely impressive.

The old way cooled data centers by evaporating water. A large campus could lose 5 million gallons a day.

Closed-loop cooling seals the water in. It circulates the same fluid over and over, and sheds the heat to the air instead of the water.

The same campus can drop to around 22,000 gallons a day.

That is genuine progress.

But closed-loop cooling does one job. It cools the servers.

It does not make a 9-gigawatt campus water-neutral.

The Wonder Valley project in Box Elder County, Utah is built on that closed-loop promise. Its application says the cooling 'will not result in a consumptive loss' of water.

For a sealed cooling loop, that can be true. But it is a statement about a pipe, not a basin.

The Great Salt Lake’s decline is driven by one thing above all: water drawn upstream before it ever reaches the lake. A 9-gigawatt campus requires massive power generation, and that power carries a water cost no cooling system can touch.

And the location is the part no cooling system can touch.

So Utah is fighting over cooling water. One water application drew 3,800 protests before the developers pulled it and refiled for a fraction.

—

The most efficient cooling system in the world cannot add water to a basin that has none.

What happens to that lake comes down to where the next one gets built.

I'm a professional water resources engineer (licensed in Utah), educated at Utah State just "over the hill" from Hansel Valley. Stratos is a proposed $100 billion AI data center generating 9 gigawatts of on-site natural gas power, nearly double Utah's current peak demand (at full build-out), and it has been pitched as "essential" to winning an AI arms race. But unfortunately, when the framing is national security and the money is measured on that scale, claims like Governor Cox's get shaped to clear a path, and simply do not describe reality.

The proposed site is almost entirely rangeland. Seasonal grazing on semi-arid ground with brackish groundwater. It is not irrigated cropland demanding 3-4 acre-feet per acre. Comparing a data center's demand against a paper water right that isn't being fully exercised is not an accurate picture of the hydrologic water balance.

To be clear, there are false claims on both sides of this issue. But even if this were irrigated farmland, the Governor's comparison would still be misleading. Irrigation across the Great Salt Lake basin returns roughly a third of diversions to groundwater, springs, and the lake as return flows. Evaporative cooling converts 70-80% of withdrawn water to vapor. It leaves the basin and doesn't come back.

Switching from agriculture to industrial cooling removes those return flows from a closed basin where the lake has already lost two-thirds of its volume. Locomotive Springs, 2 miles from the site, has lost 80% of its spring flow to pumping.

When someone says a project "uses less water," ask: less water diverted, or less water consumed? As it relates to this proposal, water, and the Great Salt Lake, that distinction IS the conversation.

Today Utah Governor Cox issued Executive Order 2026-03, "Establishing a Higher Bar for Data Center Development in Utah."

Today I published a Salt Lake Tribune op-ed, and yesterday a newsletter, arguing that Utah still had time to choose differently with the Stratos data center, and that the missing policy floor is what needs to be built.

The timing isn't coincidental: the referendum effort, the legislators raising concerns, the editorial coverage, the hundreds of Utahns who showed up at Box Elder, the other voices, all of that prompted this. The pressure deserves the credit first.

The order is genuinely the right direction. Its eight principles closely follow my Tribune and newsletter pieces: protecting the Great Salt Lake and water resources, protecting air quality and non-attainment areas, protecting ratepayers from cost-shifting, mitigating wildlife impacts, ensuring transparent public comment, and explicitly coordinating across MIDA and other agencies the May 4 Stratos approval routed around. Those principles are now state policy, signed and binding on the executive branch. That is real.

But, what, if anything, is actually constrained?

The order establishes a framework for agencies to "adhere to." It does not establish enforcement, measurable standards, timelines, or consequences. Principle (i), "water consumption is not increased and water quality is protected," is the load-bearing line. As written, it's a principle agencies should consider. As implemented, it could become a binding net-zero water standard with teeth, or language in a staff briefing nobody references after the news cycle moves on. The difference is everything, and the order doesn't choose.

The order is also forward-looking. It does not, on its face, undo or reach the already-approved Stratos project. Whether anything actually changes for Stratos depends on what DEQ, DNR, and the utility regulators do with their existing authorities.

What's not in the order is also telling. No waste heat reuse (Germany requires it; Singapore caps PUE at 1.25). No efficiency standard. No requirement that operators carry the cost of new generation and transmission they create. Nothing on behind-the-meter generation built to dodge utility regulation. Those are the gaps my Tribune piece, newsletter, and tomorrow's Seattle Times op-ed on data center waste heat all argue need to be closed.

So: the right direction, signed today, and a floor that wouldn't exist without the Utahns who pushed for it. The agencies have a mandate, the Legislature has been pointed at the relevant interim study items, and the public has been validated that this is a process in which they can participate.

But, and it's a big But,

Principles are not requirements. Requirements are not measurable standards. Measurable standards are not enforcement. The work between "the right idea" and "the operator has to meet it before breaking ground" hasn't started yet.

It needs to start now.

Most data centers look like warehouses. The Stratos project in Utah is trying to change that, and the renderings from Gensler are worth a look.

O'Leary Digital CEO Paul Palandjian said: "We want a beautiful, poetic design that belongs to the West Desert. Art and architecture are a real passion of mine, and I wanted to bring out-of-the-box thinking to a category that has almost none. Our job is to honor the place it sits in."

The master plan shows 60 data center buildings clustered across six sites, a 3,000-acre solar array capable of generating 500 MW, and a mixed-use innovation district, all designed by Gensler with a design language adjusted for the desert climate. 

Phase 1 targets 1 gigawatt of onsite power generation paired with battery storage, with most of the 40,000-acre footprint remaining undeveloped to allow continued grazing and wildlife corridors. At full buildout, the project is projected to generate $108 million annually for Box Elder County. 

The broader point here is one the industry needs to take seriously. ‘Shark Tank’ Star Kevin O’Leary Defends Massive Military Data Center Project in Utah by Kiri Blakeley

Canadian businessman and "Shark Tank" star Kevin O'Leary, known for his blunt advice to hopeful entrepreneurs, has defended himself after backlash from Utah residents who oppose his plan to build a massive, multibillion-dollar data center in the state.

"I'm pretty aware of what these concerns are," he said in a video posted to his X account that has been viewed more than 1.3 million times. "They are around air, water use, heat, noise pollution, so sustainability is at the heart of what we do."

O’Leary Digital (part of O'Leary Ventures), which is also building a $70 billion AI data center in Alberta, Canada, has partnered with Utah's Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA) for the new campus. It would span roughly 40,000 acres across three sites in a dry, rural area of the Box Elder County region north and west of the Great Salt Lake.

The project has faced intense opposition, even though the planned construction site is fairly remote, with few houses, if any, for miles. Local concerns include the impact on wildlife, and meeting the project's demand for electricity and water, which data centers consume in copious amounts.

"It's an extremely rural area to be honest with you," says Wade Hayman, an agent with KW Success Keller Williams Realty in Box Elder County. "The biggest concern for me is the water."

Hayman, who lives an hour and half away and has sold properties west of the planned site, says locals go to the area, boxed in by Old Railroad Grade Road and Hansel Valley Road, and south of Route 84, mostly to "shoot guns and shoot rabbits."

"I have mixed emotions," he tells Realtor.com®. "The way the world is going, we don't have an option not to get on board with the data centers if we want to stay on top of things. I feel the concerns of people. But the way AI is going, it's going to have to be built somewhere. It's not like it's prime real estate."

He says that, as a real estate agent: "I'm torn because it's the same argument people use with housing. People complain houses are being built on orchards, but they didn't mind when their own house was built on an orchard."

Commission meeting draws large protest

Locals came out in droves on May 4 to protest the project at a Box Elder County Commission meeting. While no public comments were officially allowed, the packed crowd loudly chanted, shouted, and jeered at the three commissioners until they finally left the stage and continued the meeting virtually.

The commission unanimously approved a resolution that would give MIDA consent to create the Stratos project area, on land owned by the Department of Defense and the Utah Trust Lands Administration, and which "may include a state-of-the-art data center."

"Today’s decision isn’t the end of the oversight process, but just the beginning," Box Elder County Commissioner Tyler Vincent said in a statement.

One of the largest AI data centers ever proposed is being built on a Utah cattle ranch. The landowners signed NDAs. The tax breaks are extraordinary. And residents never got a vote. Here's what most people are missing:

The Stratos Project — Kevin O'Leary's AI data center in Box Elder County — isn't just a tech story. It's a land story.

-It happened almost overnight. Kevin O'Leary said it himself at the approval meeting: "I heard about this opportunity just five months ago. No one has pulled this off this fast, ever."

-The landowners are ranchers — and they're keeping their cattle. Bar H Ranch and affiliated entities control roughly 16,000 acres across 33 parcels of the site. Their deal includes leaseback rights to keep ranching while the data center gets built. Grazing land one day, AI infrastructure the next.

-Very few know the actual deal terms. Sale or ground lease? The landowners are under NDA. MIDA's own documents reference "sale, lease, or development" — the structure still isn't public.

Developers also receive 100% personal property tax relief on all data center equipment and an 80% rebate on real property taxes - per the proposed interlocal agreement. Box Elder County keeps just 20 cents of every property tax dollar generated.

-A referendum has been filed. A citizens group called BEAR — Box Elder Accountability Referendum — has filed applications to put the approval to a public vote. They still need legal clearance and 5,422 signatures to qualify. Whether it makes the November ballot is still unclear. This isn't over.

Electricity generates heat—it’s basic thermodynamics. That heat radiates from whatever source is pulling power. Think of your laptop; when it runs hard, a fan blows out hot air. 

Now imagine 100,000 computer servers running in a single building 24/7, 365 days a year.

Now look at Phoenix. Already one of the hottest metropolitan areas in the country, the Valley has quietly become one of the most pervasive, fastest-growing data center hubs in the world.

And the physical footprint of this digital growth is getting harder to ignore. A recent Arizona State University study led by Dr. David Sailor revealed that air-cooled condenser arrays from local data centers create thermal plumes that raise downwind neighborhood temperatures by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit.

This isn't just a local anomaly. Up in Utah, massive proposed hyperscale projects—like the controversial Project Stratos in Box Elder County—have sparked intense environmental pushback. Climate and physics models warn that dumping that much concentrated waste heat could cause severe localized heat island spikes, raising daytime temperatures by up to 5 degrees in the surrounding high-desert valleys.

As massive tech infrastructure continues to scale across the Mountain West, we aren't just managing the digital cloud—we are managing immense amounts of physical heat. 

Balancing this exponential technological growth with regional sustainability, grid reliability, and cooling infrastructure is going to be one of our defining operational and leadership challenges.

This week, Kevin O'Leary — "Mr. Wonderful" from Shark Tank — sat down with Tucker Carlson to defend his plan to build a 40,000-acre AI data center in Utah's desert. It did not go well.

Carlson asked why Utah taxpayers should subsidize a project whose tenants include Amazon, Microsoft, and Google — some of the richest companies in the world. He asked why three county commissioners, not the voters of Utah, got to decide the fate of a project twice the size of Manhattan. O'Leary's answer: "Welcome to America, buddy." He is Canadian.

The same week, commencement speakers at two universities praised AI as "the next Industrial Revolution" — and were booed by the graduating students whose careers the technology threatens.
Something is breaking in the national consensus around the AI data center boom.

But here in Lancaster County, we already know there's a better way. Because it's happening right here — on the footprint of two abandoned printing plants, without touching a single acre of farmland, in a deregulated power market backstopped by nuclear generation, on a watershed that renews itself with every rain.

The CoreWeave campus at the former R.R. Donnelley site on Greenfield Road is proof that you don't need 40,000 acres in a desert. You need the wisdom to recognize good fundamentals when you see them.

I wrote about this in a new Substack. The argument is simple: the national model for responsible AI infrastructure may be coming from Lancaster County, Pennsylvania — from a place where horse-drawn buggies share the road with semitrucks, and where the people who live among the Amish never forgot that prudence is not the enemy of progress. It is its prerequisite.

Share it if you think the country needs to hear it.
— Kevin Lynn Executive Director, Institute for Sound Public Policy Founder, U.S. Tech Workers Member, Respect Farmland

I'm a software engineer and avid AI user. I advocate for the technology and follow the infrastructure powering it closely.

One baseline reality: we cannot build data centers fast enough right now.

Projects like the Stratos mega-campus in Box Elder County are incredibly ambitious. Because compute is rapidly becoming a commodity, these campuses are highly appealing to investors. But dropping them into a high-desert environment like Utah raises serious ecological questions.

The two primary constraints for any data center are power and cooling. The traditional approach (plug into the local grid, use evaporative water cooling towers) creates a massive double-whammy in Utah: it risks driving up electricity rates for residents and evaporates our most precious resource rather than letting it flow into our reservoirs and the Great Salt Lake.

Modern engineering has answers. On-site solar, nuclear, and next-gen geothermal can insulate the local grid. For cooling, two advanced approaches stand out:

Two-phase immersion: Servers submerged in dielectric fluid. Completely sealed, closed-loop, zero water, zero server fans, drastically reduced power draw.

Geothermal/mine heat-sink loops: Heat-transfer fluid circulates through GPU racks and deep underground, letting bedrock absorb heat passively. Energy draw is limited to simple circulation pumps.

The hurdle? Both cost significantly more upfront, lengthening investor break-even timelines. In a hyper-competitive market, developers look for shortcuts.

The Stratos site was chosen because it sits directly on the Ruby Pipeline. The plan: burn natural gas to generate up to 9 gigawatts on-site, and use closed-loop dry cooling to address water concerns. That last part successfully prevents billions of gallons from evaporating, but rejecting that much heat into dry desert air requires massive fan arrays, potentially creating a localized heat island effect in Hansel Valley.

So where do I stand?

We absolutely need to build out global AI compute. But Utah is likely the wrong place for a fossil-fuel-powered mega-campus unless developers are willing to invest in immersion cooling and clean power. Regions with abundant water, cooler climates, and grids built to absorb massive loads are far more responsible choices. My hope is that lawmakers can look past short-term tax incentives and guide these generational projects to where they make ecological sense.

As it currently stands, Stratos doesn't make sense. With serious adjustments, it could. But that comes with increased cost and risk, and until something changes, this shouldn't move forward yet absolutely must in the right ecological environment.

I spent my flight home to SF running the physics on Utah's new 9 GW data center in Substrata. What I found isn't in the permit record.

The Stratos Hyperscale Data Center [40,000 acres, 9 GW, $100 billion] is planned for Hansel Valley, a closed arid basin on the northern shore of the Great Salt Lake. The public debate has been almost entirely political: water rights, jobs, and who gets to decide what gets built on 40,000 acres of high desert. What it has not been about is the ground itself.

Three findings that aren't in the permit record:
1. The soil in Hansel Valley conducts heat at 0.22 to 0.59 W/m·K. Standard industry analysis assumes 1.4. That is a 2.5 to 7x overestimate of the ground's ability to dissipate heat, before accounting for the dry-out feedback loop that makes it worse over time.
2. In every scenario modeled, including the Phase I cap, the thermal plume crosses the water table within the 30-year operational horizon. The sediments below that line are the same ones that liquefied during Utah's only documented surface fault rupture in 1934.
3. Locomotive Springs, a federally significant wetland on the Great Salt Lake, is hydrologically connected to the same aquifer this facility will thermally load for decades. Existing curtailment triggers don't cover thermal loading. They would simply not fire.

Full analysis, figures, and technical report in the comments.

The ground doesn't wait for the permits to catch up.

"Skeptics of the proposed hyperscale data center in Box Elder County are sweating about a lot more than its energy demands and potential toll on water supplies.

"Turn out, it could create a massive heat island capable of devastating the area’s ecology, said Robert Davies, a physics professor at Utah State University.

"“I suspected it would not be good,” Davies said. “What I’ve found is it’s so much worse than I even thought it would be.”

"News of the proposed sprawling data complex, dubbed the Stratos Project, became public last month. The project’s boosters say it will likely need 9 gigawatts of energy at full build — more than double the electricity currently used by the entire state of Utah. That energy will likely come from a pipeline carrying natural gas from Wyoming to Nevada, Oregon and California. The project’s developer, “Shark Tank” celebrity Kevin O’Leary, specifically chose Box Elder County’s Hansel Valley to build the complex because the pipeline spans it, state officials have said. …

"The project will actually produce more than 9 gigawatts of energy, Davies explained, because anytime a gadget consumes power, it also produces energy in the form of heat, whether it’s a toaster, a car or a sprawling rack of computer servers. 

"All the heat the Stratos Project emits will add up to another 7 to 8 gigawatts of energy in the form of waste heat.

"Typically, waste heat is generated far from the power plant itself, in homes, businesses or on roads where it dissipates.

"But for the Stratos project, it will get dumped into the local environment of Hansel Valley, in the same geographic bowl as the power plant. That actually makes the data complex a 16 gigawatt thermal load project, the “equivalent of about 23 atom bombs worth of energy dumped into this local environment every single day,” Davies said.

“What happens if you deposit that much energy continuously into a topography like this?” Davies wondered. “Right at the north end of the Great Salt Lake, a watershed that’s in collapse. A high desert environment? A valley?”

"The professor predicts dumping that much heat and energy into Hansel Valley will raise local temperatures by five degrees Fahrenheit during the day and up to 28 degrees at night. …

"Davies also ran calculations on the Stratos Project in units of Walmart Supercenters. Its 40,000 acre-foot print is the equivalent of around 2,000 of those centers, but its energy footprint is around 2,000 Walmarts stacked 20 deep.”"

Working in the data center industry means understanding that not all data centers are created equal.

As our digital world continues to expand, the United States has developed a diverse ecosystem of data centers, each serving a specific purpose within the modern technology landscape.
🔹 Enterprise Data Centers
 These are privately owned facilities operated by a single organization to support its internal business operations. Banks, healthcare providers, manufacturers, and large corporations often rely on enterprise data centers for applications that require greater control, security, and compliance. 
🔹 Colocation Data Centers
 Instead of building and maintaining their own facility, companies can lease space, power, cooling, and connectivity within a third-party data center. Colocation has become a preferred option for organizations seeking scalability while reducing capital expenditures. 
🔹 Hyperscale Data Centers
 These are the giants of the industry. Built and operated by major cloud providers, hyperscale facilities support massive workloads, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, streaming platforms, and global digital services. Industry analysts project that hyperscalers will continue to account for the majority of future data center capacity growth. 
🔹 Edge Data Centers
 As applications increasingly require real-time processing, smaller facilities are being deployed closer to end users. Edge data centers reduce latency and improve performance for technologies such as autonomous systems, IoT devices, AI inference, and 5G networks. 
🔹 Modular Data Centers
 Built using prefabricated components, modular facilities offer rapid deployment and flexible expansion. They are becoming increasingly attractive for organizations that need capacity quickly or operate in remote locations. 

What makes this industry particularly fascinating is how these different models increasingly work together. Enterprise workloads, colocation providers, hyperscale cloud platforms, and edge deployments are becoming part of a highly interconnected infrastructure ecosystem rather than competing alternatives. 

The growth has been remarkable. Over the past decade, the industry has evolved from a predominantly enterprise-owned infrastructure model to one increasingly driven by hyperscale cloud providers, AI workloads, and edge computing. Hyperscale and colocation facilities accounted for less than 40% of U.S. server energy consumption in 2014; by 2023, that figure had risen to roughly 74%, and the U.S. data center market is projected to more than double in value by 2033. 

What was once viewed as a back-office IT function has become one of the most critical infrastructure sectors in the world. And if the last decade was defined by cloud computing, the next one will likely be defined by AI-driven data center expansion.

The Utah Clean Energy piece on the proposed Stratos data center has been circulating this week. Solid public-information work — bounding a 9 GW project's likely impacts under the two technology paths developers actually deploy today.

It got me sketching what a third path looks like.

If you drive a double-effect absorption chiller off gas turbine exhaust — straight CCHP, the same trigeneration stack hospitals and universities have run for decades — you eliminate the largest electrical parasitic in the facility. Cooling is roughly 30% of conventional data center load. For a 9 GW IT campus, that's ~2.4 GW less generation needed for the same delivered compute.

Net effect: ~25–30% lower fuel burn, CO₂, and NOx versus the CCCT scenario UCE modeled.

It's not a free lunch. Absorption rejects ~50% more heat to atmosphere than vapor compression, which makes local heat-island risk worse exactly as global emissions get better. That's a real tradeoff, not a footnote.

Just an engineer's note that there's a meaningful third scenario between "wet-cooled CCCT" and "closed-loop RICE" — and it bends most of the curves people are working with.

Anyone seen hyperscale trigen actually penciled at this scale, or is the GT lead time killing it commercially before the engineering case can be made?

Utilities are making 30-year infrastructure decisions based on demand signals that are moving on 18-month cycles.

These are still deeply early, which is precisely why the window is interesting.

That’s a structural gap.

There is a campaign underway to stop data center construction in America.

Kevin O'Leary is building one in Utah. When opposition erupted, his team started tracing where it was coming from.

What they found was not a grassroots movement.

They found coordinated spikes in social media activity traced to the same IP addresses. Bot activity. Accounts from outside the country dumping false information about water usage and grid impact. O'Leary alleged the trail ran through a U.S.-based advocacy network and ultimately back to Chinese government-connected organizations.

But here is the question that does not require any investigation to ask:

Who benefits if America stops building data centers?

Not the rural communities worried about water bills. They would benefit from the jobs, the tax base, and the economic activity. Not American workers. In Kansas City alone, the business manager of IBEW Local 124 said projected regional construction work over the next decade grew from $30 billion a few years ago to $80 billion today. Data center projects are driving that pipeline.

The entity that benefits from a slower U.S. data center buildout is the one trying to win an AI arms race against us.

Between a third and half of all U.S. data centers planned for 2026 are already expected to be delayed or canceled. Supply chain constraints are part of the problem. So is organized local opposition. Every project killed accelerates the gap.

So ask yourself: if you wanted to slow America's AI infrastructure buildout without ever touching a chip or a server, what would you do?

You would go to the local level. You would make it about water. You would make it about the power grid. You would make it feel like a community issue, not a national security one.

That is exactly what is happening.

Don't believe the claim that O'Leary's Death Star AI data center won't harm your health. Let's start with some basic medical science.

“There is no safe level of air pollution exposure.”

That’s the warning from Dr. Brian Moench, President of Utah Physicians for a Healthy Environment (UPHE), in response to claims that Utah’s growing AI data center expansion will not harm public health.

Medical research shows that even small increases in air pollution can have significant health impacts, especially for children, pregnant women, and vulnerable communities.

The relationship between pollution and disease is not linear. In fact, lower levels of exposure can produce disproportionately large health effects, as illustrated in the graph attached.

The bottom line for pollution from AI data centers: Many if not most of the 22 applications for new AI data centers in Utah will be given an air quality permit from the DAQ, because our federal and state laws are too weak to prevent their construction on that basis. But as we are seeing recently, projects of this magnitude don't come without massive friction. A critical decision vote was delayed after residents voiced concerns over transparency and the "Social Contract." The +/- $100B project now awaits a special meeting next week.

Why is this an infrastructure "Pressure Test" to watch?

- The Total Grid Exit: Stratos isn’t "plugging in", it's tapping the Ruby Pipeline for 100% on-site generation. It’s a power play taken to the max.

- Water Stewardship vs. Ag Heritage: In a water-stressed basin, 9 GW of compute is a high-stakes bet. The project is lean on non-evaporative cooling to protect the Great Salt Lake watershed, but for generational farmers, this is a hard sell.

- Scale vs. Sovereignty: With a 3 GW Phase 1 target and state-level MIDA approval in hand, the real lever isn't the capital, it’s the local permitting. 

Are we over-scaling into territory where high reward meets unprecedented risk? What will come next?

🚨🇺🇸UTAH PUSHBACK: Footage from the recent Box Elder County Commission meeting highlights the heated atmosphere surrounding the approval of the Stratos project. Residents were vocal, chanting “People over profits!” and protesting against the decision.

The backlash stems from concerns about the implications of data centers, which consume vast amounts of land, water, and energy, drive up local prices, and offer limited benefits to the community. This growing resident anger follows the unanimous approval despite the protests.

For context, the Stratos project aims to develop up to 40,000 acres in Hansel Valley, potentially becoming the world’s largest data center. Backed by Kevin O’Leary’s firm and partners, it is closely tied to the increasing demand for AI. The power requirements could reach 9 GW at full buildout, more than double Utah’s current total electricity usage, with plans for on-site natural gas generation.

Local concerns include:
- Strain on water resources in Utah’s arid climate, near the Great Salt Lake
- Land use implications
- Noise and heat generation
- Potential increases in energy costs
- A rushed approval process facilitated by the Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA) with tax incentives

Supporters, including Governor Spencer Cox and local commissioners, argue that the project will create jobs, generate tax revenue, boost the economy, and enhance U.S. competitiveness in AI against China. O’Leary has highlighted sustainability features such as air-cooling and a renewable energy mix in his other projects, leveraging his background in environmental studies.
